name: Erythrulose

lead: Erythrulose is a small sugar found in fruits such as raspberries and used in sunless tanning products, usually together with DHA. It gives a bronzed look without sun exposure, with colour that shows within hours.

It reacts with amino acids in the outer skin layer in a Maillard-type reaction to form brown pigments, more slowly than DHA. Cosmetic-industry descriptions say combining the two affects colour development and evenness, with a more gradual build and more even fade; no clinical trials of its tanning performance were found.

paras: It is applied as a lotion, mousse or spray in self-tanners, typically blended with DHA, and the colour develops over several hours. Users reapply as the tan fades over days to build or maintain colour.
The sources reviewed contain no safety or regulatory data specific to erythrulose.

angle.text: Erythrulose is a sugar used with DHA in self-tanners to give a sunless bronzed colour that appears within hours, by reacting with the outer skin layer. It is described as developing more slowly and fading more evenly; independent trials were not found.

lead: Erythrulose is a four-carbon sugar used in sunless tanning products to give skin a gradual brown colour without sun exposure. It is usually blended with dihydroxyacetone (DHA) in self-tanners, where it is used to build colour and help the tan look more natural and even.[1][2] It occurs naturally in fruits such as red raspberries and melons and is commonly produced by microbial fermentation.[1]

As a tanner, erythrulose is described as reacting with amino acids in the dead outer layer of skin in a Maillard-type reaction, producing brown pigments without changing skin melanin. It develops more slowly than DHA, and the colour fades over days as the skin sheds.[2] Brands combine the two to reduce streaking and orange tones associated with DHA alone, according to Grokipedia.[1]

A 2026 review of sunless tanners found that all 37 of the top-selling products it examined contained DHA and 38 percent also contained erythrulose; about 2 percent of customer reviews mentioned skin reactions.[3] No clinical trials of erythrulose alone were found.
infobox: Sunless tanning ingredient, often with DHA [1][2]

paras: Erythrulose is the only ketotetrose, with the formula C4H8O4 and a molar mass of about 120 g/mol. It exists as D and L forms, is a colourless, sweet-tasting, water-soluble compound, and can be made by enzyme-mediated condensation of glycolaldehyde.[1] In 2026 it was reported in a molecular cloud near the centre of the Milky Way.

Grokipedia, an AI-generated reference that may contain errors, says erythrulose reacts with amino groups in keratin to form brown pigments (melanoidins), reacts more slowly than DHA, and is blended with DHA to improve evenness and wear; it is supplied as an aqueous syrup of about 80 percent active material.[1] Wikipedia's article on sunless tanning likewise says erythrulose works similarly to DHA but develops more slowly and is often included alongside it, with the tan fading over roughly 3 to 10 days.[2]

Wikipedia's sunless tanning article reports that DHA and erythrulose can both cause contact dermatitis, that the tan itself gives no sun protection, and that the US FDA has approved DHA for external use but not around the eyes, lips or mucous membranes or by inhalation.[2] The 2026 review lists contact dermatitis and pigmentary changes among reported adverse effects of sunless tanners generally.[3]

No studies found testing erythrulose by itself. A 2026 review of sunless tanners examined product ingredients and customer reviews rather than clinical outcomes.[3] A 2017 French article on self-tanning products covers the category.[4]

timeline.event: First commercial DHA self-tanner, Man-Tan, appears; erythrulose later becomes a common companion ingredient.[2]
